questions.title: Shortest Path In A Weighted Road Graph
questions.summary: Compute the cheapest route between two nodes when every road weight is non-negative.
questions.prompt: Given a weighted graph of roads, a start node, and a target node, return the cost of the shortest route.

examples.explanation: A to C to B is cheaper than A to B directly.

constraints: Weights are non-negative integers. Path costs fit signed 32-bit integers in these examples. Return −1 for an unreachable target.

diagrams.title: Relaxation
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A((A)) -- 1 --> C((C))
  C -- 2 --> B((B))
  A -- 4 --> B

solutionTracks.title: Dijkstra With Priority Queue
solutionTracks.summary: For non-negative road weights, always expand the currently cheapest city and relax outgoing roads.

steps.title: Seed the start
steps.explanation: Distance to the start is zero and all other distances are initially unknown.

steps.title: Expand cheapest candidate
steps.explanation: A priority queue returns the unprocessed node with the smallest known distance.

steps.title: Relax edges
steps.explanation: If reaching a neighbor through the current node is cheaper, update its distance and push it into the queue.

solutionTracks.explanation: With non-negative weights, the first time a node is popped with its best distance, no future path can improve it. The priority queue enforces that safe processing order.

complexity.time: O((V + E) log(E + 2)), including stale priority-queue records

solutionTracks.title: Bellman–Ford Relaxation
solutionTracks.summary: Use repeated edge relaxation as a simple weighted baseline.

steps.title: Initialize distances
steps.explanation: Start is zero; all other nodes are unreachable.

steps.title: Relax every edge
steps.explanation: For at most V−1 passes, improve the target distance with distance[source] + weight.

steps.title: Stop and report
steps.explanation: Stop on an unchanged pass; return −1 if the requested target is still unreachable.

solutionTracks.explanation: After pass i, all paths with at most i edges have been considered. A shortest path without a negative cycle can be chosen simple and uses at most V−1 edges. Stop early when no distance improves. For this prompt weights are non-negative; BFS would be valid only when all edges have equal weight.

questions.title: Meeting Rooms II
questions.summary: Find the minimum number of rooms needed for overlapping meetings.
questions.prompt: Given meeting start and end times, return the minimum number of rooms required so every meeting can be scheduled.

examples.explanation: The first meeting overlaps each shorter meeting.

constraints: A meeting ending at time t frees the room for another meeting starting at t.
Intervals have positive duration: start < end.

solutionTracks.title: End Time Min Heap
solutionTracks.summary: Sort meetings by start time and keep a min heap of room end times to reuse rooms as soon as they free up.

steps.title: Sort starts
steps.explanation: Processing meetings chronologically lets each meeting decide whether the earliest room is already free.

steps.title: Pop free room
steps.explanation: If the smallest end time is at or before the next start, that room can be reused.

steps.title: Track heap size
steps.explanation: After adding the current end, the maximum heap size is the number of rooms required.

solutionTracks.explanation: The heap contains one next-available time per allocated room. A start can reuse the room with the earliest end; otherwise allocate a new room. Only one room needs to be reused per meeting. The heap size never decreases across iterations and equals the maximum rooms allocated. These examples sort the supplied interval array in place.

solutionTracks.title: Separate Start And End Sweep
solutionTracks.summary: Sort starts and ends independently and count simultaneous active meetings as pointers move forward.

steps.title: Sort starts and ends
steps.explanation: The next start adds a room unless the earliest end has already freed one.

steps.title: Move end pointer on reuse
steps.explanation: If a meeting ended before the next start, consume that end and reuse the room.

steps.title: Count active rooms
steps.explanation: Each unreused start increases the number of active rooms and updates the maximum.

solutionTracks.explanation: The sweep compares the next meeting arrival against the earliest departure. That is enough to know whether total concurrent meetings grows or one room is reused.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def min_rooms_sweep(intervals):
    starts = sorted(start for start, end in intervals)
    ends = sorted(end for start, end in intervals)
    used = best = end_i = 0
    for start in starts:
        if start >= ends[end_i]:
            used -= 1
            end_i += 1
        used += 1
        best = max(best, used)
    return best

questions.title: Connected Regions
questions.summary: Count groups of connected land cells in a grid.
questions.prompt: Given a binary grid where 1 is land and 0 is water, return the number of connected land regions using four-direction adjacency.

examples.explanation: The top-left cluster, bottom-left cell, and bottom-right cell are separate.

constraints: Use four-direction adjacency unless the prompt says diagonal connections count.
Input is a nonempty rectangular grid.

solutionTracks.title: Grid DFS Flood Fill
solutionTracks.summary: Treat each land cell as part of a graph and flood-fill every unseen connected component.

steps.title: Scan every cell
steps.explanation: A new region starts whenever the scan finds land that has not been visited.

steps.title: Flood neighbors
steps.explanation: DFS marks the current cell and recursively explores its four adjacent land neighbors.

steps.title: Count components
steps.explanation: Increment the region count once before each flood-fill because that fill consumes exactly one component.

solutionTracks.explanation: Connectivity is transitive: every land cell reached by the flood fill belongs to the same region. Starting a fill only from unseen land counts each region once.

solutionTracks.title: Union Find Components
solutionTracks.summary: Give every land cell an id, union adjacent land cells, and count unique component roots.

steps.title: Create ids for land
steps.explanation: Map each land coordinate to a disjoint-set id and ignore water cells.

steps.title: Union neighbors
steps.explanation: For each land cell, union it with right and down land neighbors to connect components.

steps.title: Count roots
steps.explanation: After all unions, the number of distinct roots among land ids is the number of regions.

solutionTracks.explanation: Union find stores connected components explicitly. Unioning adjacent land cells merges exactly the cells that share a region, and final roots identify distinct regions. This compact implementation uses path compression without union by rank/size. Do not claim the inverse-Ackermann bound for it. Add union by size to obtain the usual near-linear amortized bound; recursive find can otherwise be deep.

complexity.time: O(N²) conservative worst-case bound, N = rows × columns
